Parashas Mikeitz | Dec 3rd-4th 2021

Sweet Up and Down

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus 

There is a rhythm to life. We breath in and then out. We step with our right foot, and then with our left. We sleep and then we awake. We see for a moment, but then we blink. 

Our Sages stated thousands of years ago that the world is not a stagnant, fixed reality as it appears but that HaShem literally recreates the physical universe at every single moment. Recently, quantum physics has corroborated this ancient teaching, revealing that the entire world is popping into and out of existence at each instant, like the blink of an eye! 

Our Sages also teach that man is called an “Olam Katan”, a small world. Therefore, in some very profound way, we are also bursting into and out of existence. 

Until the wellsprings of the Ba’al Shem Tov began to spread forth, our understanding of this reality remained obscure. However, the Ba’al Shem Tov and the great Chassidic Masters dug down deep and pulled out the most potent parallel between the pulsating nature of man’s consciousness and the pulsating rhythm of the world. 

Chassidus explains that man’s mind is in a constant state of fluctuation between expansion and constriction. The source for the ups and downs of life comes from an inner psycho-spiritual dynamic known as “Ratzo v’Shov”, running and returning. In the famous sixth lesson of Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman utilizes his powerful understanding of “Ratzo v’Shov”, to shed light on the bipolar state of man and the key to attaining harmony with the natural ebbs and flows of our mind. 

At times Rebbe Nachman explains that we will be feeling particularly good. We will have tranquility of mind. Our emotional state will be joyful. Our actions constructive. 

This is coming from an expanded state of consciousness known as Mochin D’Gadlut. Then in one instant, our thoughts become dark, our emotions turbulent, and our actions destructive. This iscoming from a constricted state of consciousness known Mochind’Katnut. 

In the modern world, we seek psychotherapy for this pattern. However, Rebbe Nachman explains that the problem is not in the pattern itself, but how we respond to it. Put simply, in times of expanded consciousness, our orientation to life should be growth oriented and explorative, with an intense desire to achieve a greater truth than the one we currently possess. The focus being on climbing from rung to rung. 

On the other hand, when constricted consciousness strikes, we should not continue our quest for understanding and truth seeking. Instead, we should empty our minds completely of what we hold to be true, and simply believe that what is taking place is for the very best. The focus being on not getting pushed off the rung completely. 

One might scoff at such a response as being ignorant and naïve. However, the depths of this teaching runs very deep. 

How does one actually achieve greater understanding? Rebbe Nachman is telling us that when trouble strikes, your ability to “know” is purposefully concealed from you by HaShem. At this point your choice is either to resist, as we so often do, or to believe more deeply. Once one’s belief and hope deepens, his or her capacity to experience a higher truth paradoxically expands along with it. When approached correctly, the constriction of “knowing” paves the way for greater understanding.

In this week’s Parashah, Yosef ends his twenty two year long period of intense servitude and begins to become the most influential and fruitful figure in the world. While this transition might appear to be highly incongruent, it is actually Yosef’s positive response to negative circumstances that created the possibility for this sweeping transformation. 

Our Sages teach us that while in prison, Yosef was a “jumping man”. Yosef had accustomed himself to respond to his problems with dancing and singing. He did not attempt to understand the “unfortunate” circumstances of his life. Instead, he decided to face them with the utmost faith and joy. As a result, he was able to see the good in his life, and achieve greater clarity than those around him. It was with this intense clarity, that he left prison and became viceroy of the most powerful country in the world. 

Rebbe Nachman teaches that only a person who becomes expert in going up and down, can truly find his way back to HaShem, and bring everyone along with him. 

Yosef’s ability to go up and down successfully ultimately led to his own personal redemption as well as that of everyone around him. 

May HaShem bless us to know how to run and return like Yosef HaTzaddik, facing our challenges with strength, simplicity, and joy, and responding to our successes with an ever growing yearning for greater understanding and clarity. With this, we will find our way back to the One who loves us so dearly and waits longingly for our true arrival. 

Shabbat Shalom.

Light at the Heart of Darkness

Aaron London, RN, BSN

In the 5765 printing of De’ah Chochma L’Nafshecha, Rav Yitzchak Meir Morgenstern writes that the essential spiritual work of Chanukah is to bring down light into the lowest places (p. 140). Based on the writings of Reb Nosson from Breslov, in sefer Likutey Halachos, Orach Chaim, Hilchos Shabbos, Halachah Vav, Section 25, he elucidates this idea specifically within the context of the tzaddik, whose primary task is to descend to the impoverished place of everyday people in order to ignite their inner worlds with “holy fire” for Hashem (p. 140). 

In a similar vein, R’ Zvi Aryeh Rosenfeld, in his exposition of Rebbe Nachman’s Sichos HaRan, explains that the greatness of the true tzaddik is not how high he can ascend, but rather how he can travel “to the depth and bowels of the earth… in order to elevate and bring back a person who has gone so far” (Rebbe Nachman’s Soul, Volume 1, p. 21). 

With the above framework in mind, I would like to share two points which I think can deepen as well as humanize our avodas Hashem. Sefer Yishiah teaches us that the Jewish people are all tzaddikim (60:21). In other words, there is an essential place within every Jew which is completely righteous, irrespective of one’s behavior. Perhaps, this is also the concept of the neshama, which is the animating force of G-dliness within every Jew that cannot be tarnished in any way. 

If we understand that there is an irreducible point of tziddkus within each of us, then the avodah of the tzaddik can apply to us as well. That is to say, each one at his or her own level can 

engage meaningfully in the practice of descending into darkness in order to ignite the flames of spiritual light – the light of hope, the light of healing, the light of emunah that is specifically nurtured within the spaces of human experience that are darker, where Hashem’s presence is often not felt. 

Thus, one expression of the inner tzaddik is in our movement towards helping another person believe that the shadows of his or her humanity are not contrary to G-dliness, but rather the authentic place where G-dliness is experienced. One of the most important ideas for a person to internalize is that one’s humanity is the place of possibility, not despair. 

However, for so many people, especially the people I work with in substance abuse, the more they come in contact with the seemingly darker parts of their personality, the more hopelessness they feel. When I can share that space of initial hopelessness with somebody and help him see that what appeared to be hopeless is really hopeful, then I have actualized the avodah of Chanukah.

Indeed, this is what I believe our tzaddikim are sharing with us. The avodah of Chanukah is the avodah of believing that darkness does not have be the place of despair, but rather the place of hope and potential and healing. Imperfection, in all its expressions, is not the end. It is the beginning. As we see with Yosef himself, his resilience emerged out of his awareness that, no matter what transpired, Hashem was with him. Therefore, what comes out are two aspects of the avodah. One aspect is our relationship with other people in helping them shift how they experience their humanity. The second aspect is in relation to ourselves. That, so-to-speak, our inner tzaddik is able to descend into the dark crevices of our personality, only to show that Hashem has been waiting for us there all along. 

At that lowest meeting point, between us and Hashem, it is simply the awareness that He is there which serves as the most healing light of all. 

Parashas Vayeishev | Nov 26th-27th 2021

The Dreamer 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

For anyone who’s ever had a dream, he or she knows that the path to actualizing that dream is filled with obstacles and barriers. And while the dreamer is celebrated and romanticized, the truth is that a real dreamer must be a fearless warrior, willing to endure unfathomable hardships and resistance to achieve what he or she believes in. 

In this week’s Parashah, we learn for the first time about the dreamer, Yosef, and his courageous journey towards fulfilling his lofty dreams. 

Yosef was different. He was naive. He lacked awareness of what was considered “normative”. He acted in ways that weren’t socially acceptable. 

And when Yosef began to verbalize his fantastical dreams, Yosef’s brothers found his grandiosity to be off-putting and even threatening. So much so that they began to harbor intense hatred and jealousy towards their youngest brother. 

None of this stopped Yosef from chasing his dreams. 

For despite the alienation and cruelty from the brothers whom he loved, Yosef understood that fulfillment of his dreams would be the fulfillment of the deepest yearning of his brothers as well. 

But despite Yosef’s prodigious nature and pure intentions, in one moment, his entire life was turned upside down. 

Not recognizing the consequences of being so thoroughly hated, he innocently chased his brothers into the field and before he knew it, was stripped of his garments and thrown into a pit. 

His brothers deliberated the possibility of ending his life but 

ultimately decided on selling him into the servitude of foreigners. 

Yosef was sold four times before he began his period of slavery in Mitzrayim. There, he was falsely accused and sent into prisonfor over a decade. 

Like many who have endured trauma, abuse, bullying, or suddenloss, what appeared at first to be the story of a promising young man with unlimited potential and a good heart, quickly unraveled into a nightmare of unspeakable proportions. 

Yosef’s life prospects crumbled before his eyes and his family fell apart from the grief of a lost son. 

Yet through all of this, there had been one missing piece. One glaring omission. 

Where the heck is G-d? 

Where is HaShem in the midst of such horror and atrocity? 

In one of the most powerful and poignant teaching of our Oral Torah, the Sages expounded “Yosef’s brothers were preoccupied with the selling of Yosef. Reuven was preoccupied with his sackcloth and fasting. Yaakov was preoccupied with hissackcloth and fasting. Yehuda was preoccupied with taking a woman (cohabiting with a prostitute), and HaShem was creating the light of the Mashiach.” 

In what had appeared to be the complete disintegration of Yosef’s personal life and that of his family, HaShem had orchestrated this entire upheaval only in order to bring about the fulfillment of Yosef’s dreams. For in truth, they were His dreams as well. 

At this time, six years ago, I was sitting by the light of my Chanukia, reading Tehillim, and crying over the intense emotional distress and relentless psychological turmoil I had experienced in the years since becoming Ba’al Teshuva. 

Rebbe Nachman’s teaching from Likutey Moharan was playing over and over in my mind, “It may appear that all your efforts and attempts are being rebuffed and rejected on High. It may be days, months, or even years that you feel HaShem simply isn’t interested in your service. In truth, all distancing is only for the sake of being brought close.” 

With tears in my eyes, I begged HaShem, “I don’t even need you to help me. I’ve given up on that. I just need you to show me that Your are with me. And if I’m not who I believe I am, just tell me already, so I can stop fighting for this.” 

That night, I had a dream. 

I don’t feel comfortable yet to discuss the contents of that dream. But it became clear to me that HaShem was with me. And that my lifelong dreams weren’t mine alone, but they were His as well. 

And just as Yosef before me, the seemingly catastrophic events in my life had served as the unlikely catalyst to begin the genuine fulfillment of my lifelong dreams. 

Rebbe Nachman once stated that the greatness of HaShem lies in fact that He can take the most calamitous challenges of a person’s life, and transform them into his personal bliss. 

With that message, I exhort all of my dear brothers and sisters reading this. No matter how bleak. No matter how hopeless. You must never give up. 

For the greatness of HaShem is His ability to “turn all of your meniot into neimot.” 

So dream and don’t give up. 

Because maybe, just maybe, HaShem has the very same dream. Shabbat Shalom. 

Hope at the Heart of Connection

Aaron London, RN, BSN

In his shiur based on the teachings of the Nesivas Shalom, R’ Avi Fishoff, founder of TWiSTED Parenting – an 

organization which helps parents with children experiencing “stage 4” psycho-emotional crisis – offers the following insight into this week’s parshah. 

The Midrash explains that, on his own, it was not within Yosef’s capacity to overcome the test he encountered with Potifar’s wife. Therefore, as the gemara in Sotah teaches, Yosef was able to transcend the test through seeing the image of his father’s face. The Nesivas Shalom emphasizes that, at 

the moment Yosef confronted the test, he felt totally alone. It was specifically within his aloneness that the yetzer hara (the proclivity within every Jew towards evil) overwhelmed Yosef 

in a way that was above nature. It was only through seeing the image of his father, and therefore, feeling connected to his father that ultimately strengthened Yosef to overcome the test. The essential point is as follows: the capacity for a human to being to transcend the tests of his life is rooted in his ability to transform the emotional experience of aloneness, which so many of us often feel, to the experience of connectivity. 

R’ Fishoff, based on the Nesivos Shalom, accentuates that if Yosef imagined the face of his father and experienced thoughts that Yaakov did not love him, then the possibility of transforming aloneness to connection would have been lost and Yosef would have, G-d forbid, succumbed to the test. R’ Fishoff shared a connected teaching from the Chasam Sofer which explains that Yaakov specifically gave Yosef the special multi-colored robe, not to show favoritism, but rather to strengthen his son. Yaakov understood that Yosef, as opposed to his brothers, was going to feel alone and marginalized. Therefore, Yaakov offered the robe to Yosef in order that Yosef should feel even within aloneness itself he was not alone. His father loved him. Therefore, when Yosef conjured the image of Yaakov within his inner world, he simultaneously opened himself up to the world of connectivity that energized his ability to subdue the yetzer hara. 

I worked with a patient recently, a former Army Ranger, caught in the counterfeit experience of connection which substance abuse offers, who said to me that his most recent withdrawal left him feeling the most scared he has ever felt in his life. This was a man who experienced the horrors of combat over multiple deployments. Yet, while his traumas absolutely intensified the fear he felt, the existential aloneness is what shackled him to hopelessness. He had no father to think about. Therefore, the possibility of connection which rests at the center of healing, was closed off. 

However, once in treatment, those shackles of hopelessnessbegan to break. Treatment offered this man the opportunity to connect with people who chose to care about his success – the first responders team, the social workers, the nurses, the doctor – all offered the possibility for relationship. EverydayI had the privilege of working with him, I saw his eyes shine with new hope. 

Herein lies the point – every moment we share with another human being can offer that person the possibility of connectivity. That is to say, the same way Yosef thought of his father and felt connected to his father and was, therefore, able to overcome his test, so too are we able to be the “Yaakov” to somebody else’s “Yosef.” At the heart of every encounter lies the opportunity to help a person transform the experience of aloneness to the experience of relationship. It is within the experience of connection itself which rejuvenates one’s ability to taste even the hope that was at one time impossible. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY 

Parashas Vayishlach | Nov 19th-20th 2021

Freedom 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

The most crippling part of struggle, both physical and psychological, is the deep rooted belief that you and I are victims. Each painful life experience furthers incapacitates us, reinforcing the core belief of victimhood. Over the course of time, we subconsciously build up this invisible, larger than life, state-of-the-art prison of helplessness from which most find it impossible to ever truly escape. 

The main lesson which HaShem is desperately and repeatedly trying to impart to His beloved children throughout the entire Torah is “cheirut“, freedom. It’s a Mitzvah from the Torah to remember each and every day, “I am HaShem, your G-d, that took you out of slavery”. The depth of this Mitzvah is not to emphasize the collective, historical servitude of the Jewish people in Egypt from which we were ultimately released. 

Instead, it is a deeply personal divine command to be fiercely and unapologetically empowered. 

That at every waking moment of your life, regardless of the dark and painful places you have been to, you are free! 

Rebbe Nachman teaches that the greatest spiritual impurity is not moral or even religious, it’s despair itself. 

Why did Rebbe Nachman scream in a loud voice “Ein Shum Yeush B’Olam Klal”, there is no such thing as despair in the world at all? He should have just said it or even whispered it. Rebbe Nachman needed to scream it, because despair is a lie. So he screamed it. 

Yes, it’s a juicy lie. Yes, it’s a gripping lie. Despair enthralls and captivates us. But nonetheless, it’s still a lie. And a lie can mamash kill you. It almost killed me. 

Growing up with numerous debilitating episodes of depression and anxiety, I had become accustomed to feeling powerless. It lead to countless therapists, numerous psychiatrists, and endless experimentation with psychotropic medications. The side effects of these medications and psychiatric interventions have, to this very day, sapped me of my physical energy and mental clarity. In fact, those side effects put me into a greater state of despair than the original psychological distress itself! 

But then HaShem whispered, you’re not a slave anymore. And then the Sages stated matter of factly that giving up is forbidden. And finally Rebbe Nachman screamed, despair doesn’t even exist! 

My inner voice of disempowerment began to truly change when I read this week’s Parsha, Vayishlach, for the first time. 

Yaakov struggles interpersonally with his brother Esav his entire life, from the womb until the grave. Rebbe Nachman teaches that Yaakov represents the Jew’s capacity for joy whereas Esav is the embodiment of sadness. Their lifelong struggle is actually reflective of our intrapersonal battle for happiness. 

The culmination of this war is when Esav physically throws Yaakov down to the ground and in the process threatens to end his very existence. At the moment that all hope appears 

utterly lost, Yaakov flips Esav into submission, causing Esav to beg Yaakov to release him. 

What took place next is what stunned me and ultimately changed me.

Yaakov refuses to let Esav go. 

“I won’t release you until you bless me,” Yaakov roared. 

Can you imagine? Your darkest skeleton in your closet. Your greatest trauma. Your deepest fear. Your most acute pain. They come to you and say “You win, let me go”. 

How much would you pay to release him? How much would you give up to finally let him go? 

But Yaakov is teaching the most essential of all lessons. 

Our problems are not to cripple us until we have the merit to move beyond the pain. 

No. 

Our darkness is to be cast into submission and then transformed into light itself. Our darkness is meant to “bless us”. 

Rebbe Nachman states that there is a higher form of joy than happiness itself. It’s when one transforms his own feelings of sadness into joy itself. This, the Tzaddik teaches us, is the greatest bliss. 

To go from Yaakov, meaning “the heel”, to Yisrael, “the one who fights with the Divine” and emerges victorious. 

It’s this paradigm shift that encouraged me to add the name Yisrael to the beautiful name my parents gave me at birth, and to forge forward with conviction and courage. 

I’m not a slave. I’m free. 

Now. 

Always. 

Forever. 

And so are you. 

I love you and thank you for listening to me. 

Shabbat Shalom. 

Presence and Process 

Aaron London, RN, BSN 

In the writings of Likutei Yam HaChochmah al HaTorah on this week’s parashah, Rav Itche Meir Morgenstern describes one of the foundational points in avodas Hashem. He explains, “But the path of Esav, the kelipos, is to jump to the lead – then boasting of his great power and abilities – and seeking immediately to grab all levels at one.” The path of kedushah, on the other hand, “is to go from step to step, and not to jump to high levels so fast.” Or, said slightly differently, the concept of Esav, as my teacher Rav Gerzi related to me, is the concept of future thinking that removes a person from the moment for the sake of some self-serving goal that has yet to be. In contrast, Yaakov is the concept of tifferes/emes which is the concept of presence that is anchored in authentic connection – connection with self, with the other, and with Hashem. 

With the above dynamic in mind, we can see how Western culture flows out from an Esav paradigm – results, which are future-oriented, are championed over process, which is presence-oriented. We are obsessed with destination and our proclivity towards perfectionism can further complicate our ability to abide with a sense of okay-ness in the one dimension of human experience we truly have – right now. 

Therefore, presence and process, establish the essential groundwork necessary for serving Hashem in a healthy way. 

However, despite their essential nature, presence and process are perhaps the two ingredients that are lacking the most in how we connect to Hashem, other people, and ourselves. 

What, then, is the sod of returning back to the moment in a such a way that I breathe new life into my awareness of process-centered living? How do we re-establish the paradigm of Yaakov? 

The question has been asked by many, but I would like to share with you an insight that emerged from the work I did with my nursing group this past week. 

Stuck-ness is the antithesis of presence and we often feel stuck – in a thought, in an emotion, in behaviors that do not serve us. We can often feel claustrophobic within the privacy of our own hearts.

However, just because I am stuck now does not mean I will be stuck in a moment from now. I wanted to teach my patients that they did not need to be subservient to the natural ebbs and flows of their inner worlds. They could sing and dance. The impulse of the body might be to remain seated. But I wanted them to know they could get up. Their emotional sense might be blunted. But they still could sing and dance. So I got up in the middle of group, somewhat unexpectedly (although I did warn them something strange was about to happen and not to judge me) and began to clap and sing. “See,” I began, “The moment might have a certain momentum. However, even though the moment was moving in one direction, I can still unstuck myself. You are not stuck.” Sometimes, we have to thrust ourselves into presence, electrify ourselves out of drudgery. Then, with breathlessness and opened eyes, we can, as R’ Joey Rosenfeld often mentions, serve Hashem anew in this moment and recognize that it is precisely this moment where process is experienced. Then, with a sense of menuchas hanefesh as R’ Itche Meir suggests, go one foot in front of the other towards Hashem, only to find that He is with us every step of the way. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY

Parashas Vayeitzei | Nov 12th-13th 2021

G-d is Inside of You

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus 

I once had a student who suffered from tremendous internal doubts about his faith. He rarely spoke in class and it was fairly difficult to gauge what was going on inside of him. One day, he stopped showing up entirely. 

I tried reaching out to him over the course of a few weeks to see how he was doing, but he didn’t pick up his phone or respond to my messages. I continued to pray for him every day, hoping that he would find whatever it was that he was looking for. 

Purim was right around the corner, and he was still no where to be found. However, when my students put together a Purim party, he showed up unexpectedly. 

He approached me with a huge smile on his face and thanked me deeply. I never saw him smile like that. 

He proceeded to open up to me for the first time about his lifelong difficulties with believing in HaShem, as well as his more recent challenges in connecting to the teachings of Rebbe Nachman. He told me that he had essentially given up on Judaism and this was the real reason why he stopped coming to class. 

However, he felt bad about the fact that the one plan of action I advocated so strongly for, he could never push himself to do. Finally, he told me that before he gives up on HaShem completely, he felt it was only fair to follow through with Rebbe Nachman’s main piece of advice. 

One hour of Hitbodedut. 

No distraction. No interruption. 60 consecutive minutes of secluded personal conversation with the Creator of the universe, like He is your best friend (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 25). 

My student explained that during the first 45 minutes, he felt absolutely nothing. However, in the last fifteen minutes, he started to feel an ever increasing wave of peacefulness and tranquility come over him. Finally, when he reached the 60 minute mark, he stated with tremendous enthusiasm, “For the first time in my life, I saw G-d!” 

What makes Hitbodedut the ultimate mechanism for experiencing the awesome reality of HaShem? 

Why did Rebbe Nachman so frequently “pound the table” for this unique universal practice? 

In this week’s Torah portion, “VaYeitzi”, we find the answer. 

As Yaakov Avinu was departing from his home, looking to establish his personal path in spirituality, he decided to engage in the unique practice passed down by his father and grandfather in theexact place that they had practiced it. Following a long journey to Beit El, Yaakov had his first documented session of Hitbodedut. 

Following a life changing, out of body experience, the Torah states that Yaakov entered a state of rapture and exclaimed, “HaShem is right here, and I didn’t know it!”. 

In a remarkable lesson in Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman describes the mechanics of Hitbodedut and the source of its tremendous efficacy. 

When a Jew secludes himself from society and it’s external trappings, while concurrently speaking to HaShem for an extended and uninterrupted period of time, he or she experiences a psycho spiritual state of ego-dissolution (Likutey Moharan, 52).

One’s lower self, the ego, which is comprised of the powerful pursuit for temporary pleasure, the desire for external admiration, and fear of extraneous forces, melts away entirely. The “Neshama”, one’s higher, innermost self, rises to the forefront, knocking one into a powerful state of G-d consciousness previously unexperienced. 

This powerful state of self nullification known as “Bitul”, is the hallmark of the Baal Shem Tov’s novel spiritual path known as Chassidut. The Baal Shem Tov’s great grandson, Rebbe Nachman, states matter of factly that the only way to reach this genuine state of “Bitul”, is through Hitbodedut. 

My student, as his ancestor Yaakov before him, came to the same conclusion, “How awesome is this place! This is nothing other than the House of HaShem. This is the gate to Shamayim!” 

Rebbe Nachman teaches that Avraham Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “mountain”, a challenging terrain for the courageous minority to climb. Yitzhak Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “field”, less arduous and more accessible, but still off-limits to the majority. Yaakov Avinu however, saw Hitbodedut as a “home”, the ultimate safe space and place of inner comfort, one needed and desired equally by all. Once Hitbodedut becomes a universal practice of humanity, Jew and non-Jew alike, Rebbe Nachman states that we will be privy to the Redemption and coming of Mashiach (Likutey Moharan, 10). 

I encourage everyone to take this advice to heart and find one hour during Shabbat to pour out your heart to HaShem in your own words, like He is your best friend, and bring that state of 

Geula closer. With this you will begin to find the home you always yearned for but never truly believed existed. 

As HaShem himself states in His Torah, “Build Me a home and I will dwell in them”. 

That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you. 

Shabbat Shalom. 

“That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you.”

-Rabbi Kalmus

Eyes Open, Eyes Closed

Aaron London, BSN, RN 

Rabbi Yosef Ergas, in sefer Shomer Emunim, which serves as an introduction to Kabbalah, conveys a foundational idea related to the narratives contained within the Torah. He writes, “There is no doubt that in truth, apart from the objective that is derived from the straightforward meaning of those stories about moral behavior like all other historical accounts, there must also be a powerfully [deep] objective in the stories, to hint at great secrets and the ideas related to all the true branches of wisdom” (p. 158, from R’ Avinoam Fraenkel’s translation). 

The aforementioned point roots us in a principle we discussed in last week’s article: while the basic text is offering us insight into the stories of our Avos and Immos, a deeper reading yields insight into the dynamics that play out within our own inner worlds. Rabbi Ergas writes further, “In the end, with the entire Torah, the text talks in terms of the lower worlds [this physical world], but it hints at the supernal worlds…” (p. 164). 

As we mentioned last week based on a conversation I had with my teacher, Rabbi Gerzi, “the Ari HaKodesh in Shaar Gilgulim, Perek Aleph relates that the four spiritual universes – Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiah – exist not only in the cosmic sense as a reality outside of the self, but also in a psychological sense that exist within the self” (London, “The Chumash Within”). Therefore, if the text of the Torah “hints at the supernal worlds” and our tzaddikim teach that the supernal worlds also exist as modes of consciousness, then we can understand that the text of the Torah is inviting us to experience our Avos and Immos, not just as personalities, but as psychological modes of being as well. 

With the above introduction in mind, let us now move inwards, towards the ‘Leah’ that exists at the core of our human experience. Rabbi Y.Y. Jacobson, in his article, “Do You Know Who You Married?,” conveys the following point in regards to marriage: “‘Leah’, a name that literally means “one who is weary”, represents those elements in our spouse that are more complicated, perplexing and disturbing. Leah, the weak-eyed sister, weakened from tears and anxiety, embodies our continuous and exhausting struggle with the dark demons and ugly impulses in our lives.” 

While Rabbi Jacobson is referring to the ‘Leah’ within one’s spouse, I think it is clear that the concept of ‘Leah’ exists also within ourselves. 

The Torah characterizes Leah’s eyes as tender. Our eyes are tender as well. We also cannot stop crying. 

Rashi explains that the reason Leah could not stop crying was because “she was under the impression that she was destined to ascend to the lot of Esau” (p. 322, Artscroll translation). 

Leah was not married to Esav, and yet, the fear of the possibility was enough to have the Torah define Leah by her wearied, crying eyes. Is that not the condition of anxiety today – running away from something that is not even there? 

In the midst of our tears, Rebbe Nachman whispers to us a secret: “Close your eyes,” he says. In Torah 65 of sefer Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman explains that when a person is undergoing suffering, he has to close his eyes completely from the experience of being in this world. He has to close off all external stimuli and soften into the darkness of the inner world. It is precisely that darkness which provides the possibility to see with the strong, inner eye – the eye that perceives that truly everything is from Hashem and everything Hashem does is to invite us into a more profound experience of goodness. The concealment of Hashem’s light we experience with eyes open becomes the revelation of Hashem’s light with eyes closed. Then, when we gaze at the aspect of ourselves called ‘Leah’, all the darker parts of ourselves shine with the possibility of renewed healing. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY

Shalom is the Highest 

Expression of Emet

Alex Aminov 

In this week’s parsha we read about Yaakov venturing out on his own. Taking his journey to find his wife, unable to return home where his bloodthirsty, twin brother Esav is ready to kill him for taking Issac’s blessing. There are many perplexing questions here. Firstly, the famous question, how could Yaakov, the tzaddik, the “ish taam”, man of simplicity do such a thing? After all, when we think of a man of holy simplicity, we would assume he’s someone who’s straightforward, never lying or attempting clever tricks. Another question that’s perplexed me is, why go through any of this in the first place? Why slight your brother and trick your father to end up impoverished and on the run when it was your blessing to receive in the first place. Why not just come up to Isaac and say, “Esav has sold me his birthright, he has no rights to it now. I am now considered your firstborn, please bless me as such.” In fact, that’s exactly the approach I’d expect from an “ish taam”, just being forthright and simple about the truth. Why go through all this? 

Well, a deeper “truth” may lie in Rav Nachman’s teachings to help shed some light on the perplexing behavior of our holy forefather. Rav Nachman explains there are different levels of truth. In our society, we were raised to believe that there’s the truth, and then there’s a lie. 

But according to chasidut, there are lies, then truths, then different ascending levels of higher truths. For example, when Rabbi Natan (Rabenu’s main student), was finally 

offered his dream job of being chief Rabbi of his town, he came to Rav Nachman for advice on whether he should take the position. Rav Nachman said, “it’s an amazing position, you’re perfectly suited for it, there’s no better fit than you, and the entire community will benefit immeasurably from you being rabbi.” This made Rabbi Natan very happy to hear, as he held Rabenu’s advice in very high regard. But then Rabbi Natan thought to himself, “Wait, Rabbi Nachman taught me that there’s the truth, then there’s the “truth of truths”. 

Rabbi Natan asked Rabbi Nachman “is that the truth?” Rabeinu responded “Yes”. Then he followed up with, “But is it the truth of truths?” Rabeinu responded: “No, the truth of truths is you will gain much more learning by me and working on writing and spreading my teachings.” 

Rabbi Natan listened to Rabbi Nachman, despite the fact that it meant walking away from his longtime dreams and desires for himself. And we’re glad he did today. Because Rabbi Nachman was right. Had he taken that position he would not have spread the teachings that have a massive global effect we see today. Millions of people, Jews and non-Jews alike benefit immeasurably from these teachings for over two centuries.

These teachings have brought people peace, emuna, tshuva, closeness with God, better relationships, and have even pulled people out of the brink of suicide. There’s the truth, then there’s the truth of truths. And what does Rabbi Nachman say is the highest level of truth? – Shalom, aka peace. It’s also one of HaShem’s names. It doesn’t just mean when there’s no war. It refers to the Kabbalistic expression of Godliness where HaShem is able to make two paradoxical opposing forces in harmony with each other. 

This means (going contrary to what many people would think), bending the truth for the sake of peace would technically be a higher truth than being outright and honest if it means I am hurting someone or making a big fight. Because there’s the truth and then there’s the truth of truths. The truth is that it was Yaakov’s birthright, he can demand it. But that means coming to his father and telling him his dear firstborn son Esav, a relationship Isaac treasures, sold his firstborn status for some soup. “That’s how much Esav values your blessing and being your firstborn.” Perhaps this would have broken Issac’s heart. But it’s the truth?! Yes, but then there’s the truth of truths, which is peace. Yaakov went against his simple nature to do something very out of character and send him running for his life but he stuck to the truth of truths. 

When Leah was put in Rachel’s place at her wedding, she was quiet. But wasn’t this supposed to be her husband? She had every right to speak up, this was a terrible injustice. That’s the truth. But the truth of truths is that it’s better to remain quiet than to embarrass her sister. And thank HaShem for Rachel remaining quiet, because Leah marries Yaakov and has Yehuda, from whom comes Moshiach. The geula of the world could rest on just one person – one time deciding to forgo the truth and seek out Shalom – the truth of truths, even if it means letting go of what we think we are owed, because HaShem wants to give us so much more.

Parshas Toldos | Nov 5-6 2021

Crossing the Narrow Bridge

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

“These are the children of Yitzhak, the son of Avraham. Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.

These are the opening words of Parshat Toldot, and they contain a very profound secret.
Often in life, we feel alone. Troubled by the lack of apparent good in in our personal lives and chaos in the world at large, we can’t help but wonder, “Is there really a G-d watching over us?” And even if there is, “Does He actually care about me?”

Adding to the difficulty is the Torah’s novel assertion and foundational principle that everything that takes place in one’s life is nothing other than the constant unfolding and revelation of the Infinite Oneness of HaShem.

The preeminent Italian Kabbalist, Moshe Chaim Luzzato, states in his classic work Da’at Tevunot, that the purpose and destination of our lives is to experience the ecstasy of recognizing the absolute Unity of HaShem permeating all of reality and history.

Rebbe Nachman says that one can actually achieve this in their lifetime, and in doing so, experience a taste of “The World to Come” while still in this world (Likutey Moharan, 4).

It all sounds beautiful, and far be it from me to deny the insights of our spiritual masters, but why does life so often point to the contrary?
Depression, anxiety, anger, confusion, illness, abuse, trauma. That’s only what’s going on inside me. In society, there is hatred, jealousy, manipulation, oppression, apartheid, genocide.
How can one manage to recognize Unity in such brokenness?

Comes the Torah to teach us, “Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.”
In Kabbalah, Avraham represents the profound experience of the Infinite light of HaShem permeating all of physical reality, without any concealments or obstructions.
This was Avraham’s spiritual essence and this elevated state of consciousness is what Avraham brought to the world.

Yitzhak, on the other hand, represents the complete opposite. Not the wondrous experience of revelation, but the overwhelming concealment of this Infinite light.
Yitzhak’s time was oft spent in complete solitude, engaged in the laborious work of excavating wells which his father had previously dug up. Yitzhak was kicked out from the only place he had achieved sustained success in adulthood. He lost his eye sight in his elder years and saw his favorite child take a turn for the worst prior to his passing. In the end, Yitzhak’s life was not one of self-development, but one of self-sacrifice. 

Therefore, the Torah is teaching us a paradigm shift of the highest order. 

It is HaShem’s Infinite love itself, called “Avraham”, that gives birth to the very concealment of that love, “Yitzhak”. 

Put simply, when a father loves his child, he teaches him or her how to walk. Hand in hand they embrace and traverse across the floor.

But when he loves his child even more, he lets go. In doing so, his child can learn to walk on his or her own, this being the greatest expression of love. 

The child doesn’t feel this way because he or she is not old enough to know their father’s real intentions. They also don’t possess enough awareness to appreciate the tremendous closeness of their father, even after having let go. 

Therefore, HaShem gave us the Torah. So that even in the midst of our extended period of separation and lengthy exile, we can get a window into the true intentions that preceded our current fractured state. 

That is, that “Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.” 

Love itself gave birth to distance and separation. 

As a result, the bridge of life often feels incredibly narrow. 

Notwithstanding, Rebbe Nachman stated empathically that the main thing is not to be afraid at all (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 42). 

Soon enough, Mashiach will reveal the truth. 

Each personal journey provided unique tailor-made opportunities to cultivate growth and relationship that would be impossible without the possibility of challenge and adversity. 

All of this is covertly reflected in Yitzhak’s name. Yitzhak is the future-form of the Hebrew word “tzchok”, laughter. Interestingly, Yitzhak means “he will laugh”. He doesn’t laugh now. At least not fully. 

But when his eyes regain their pristine strength and he sees the eternal joy that his self-sacrifice gave birth to, Yitzhak and all of us crossing the very narrow bridge of life

will have “mouths that are filled with laughter”. 

May it be truly soon in our days, amen. 

“Each personal journey provided unique tailor-made opportunities to cultivate growth and relationship that would be impossible without the possibility of challenge and adversity. ” -Rabbi Kalmus

The Chumash Within

Aaron London, BSN, RN 

R’ Aryeh Kaplan, in his remarkable work entitled Chasidic Masters, relates the following: “While the earlier Kabbalah tried to bring man into heaven, the main idea of Hasidism was to bring heaven into man” (4). Let us spend a few moments excavating the aforementioned point. 

Perhaps, one of the most essential chiddushim that emerged from the school of the Baal Shem Tov was that the most esoteric concepts can be experienced on the level of one’s own personal avodas Hashem. 

As one of my teachers shared with me recently, the Ari HaKodesh in Shaar Gilgulim, Perek Aleph relates that the four spiritual universes – Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiah – exist not only in the cosmic sense as a reality outside of the self, but also in a psychological sense that exist within the self. Every Jewish individual, therefore, can experience his or her own inner Olam HaAtzilus, which is considered one of the highest dimensions that the Arizal revealed to us. This is an idea R’ Joey Rosenfeld also expands upon in shiur 15 (‘Each Person is His Own Universe’) in his series of shiurim entitled “Entering the Sea of Wisdom,” which are based on the teachings of Rav Yitzchak Meir Morgenstern from Yerushalyim. 

In a similar vein, there is a principle that the narratives of the Chumash are not just historical events or the stories of our Forefathers or even moral lessons for time immemorial (even though these points are true). Rather, we can approach the stories of our Avos and the dynamics between them through a psychological lens. 

With the above principle in mind, I want to suggest the following idea which I think yields a fascinating insight into the human experience. 

Our sages teach us that that the Avos correspond to different middos. Avraham, as we know, corresponds to chesed, Yitzchak to gevurah, and Yaakov to emes/tiferes. Esav corresponds to the middah of Yitzchak, but in a corrupted way. Perhaps, we can say, Esav is the unhealthy expression of Yitzchak’s middah of gevurah, similar to Yishmael correlating to the unhealthy expression of Avraham’s middah of chesed.

Let us now look at an aspect of this week’s parsha through the psycho 

emotional lens. The Torah explains, “Yitzchak loved Esav…” (Bereshis 

25:28). Or, said differently, the middah of Yitzchak – gevurah, which 

connotes the concept of judgement/boundaries/internality – loves the middah of Esav – the middah or proclivity towards the corrupted expressions of gevurah, such as criticism, meanness, hatred, etc. Rashi explains that the reason Esav returned home from the field exhausted was because he was worn out from murdering, which is perhaps the most severe manifestation of gevurah (Rashi on pasuk 29). 

There is a subtle point I want to draw our attention towards and it is a point that I often see with the people I work with who suffer from substance abuse. It is a point that exists for most of us in varying intensities. 

The idea of Yitzchak loving Esav is the idea of our own tendency towards “loving” habits and behaviors which are unhealthy. Not because there is something wrong with us, but rather we comfortably abide in those behaviors which have been reinforced over time. In a very real way, a person can feel more at home with the inner critical voice than the inner voice of self-forgiveness. Within one’s own space of internality (Yitzchak) he retains a negative bias towards the aspects of self rooted in Esav. 

Nevertheless, there is the aspect of self which is called Yaakov. Yaakov, who corresponds to truth, balance, simplicity, and wisdom. And, within every Jewish individual, is this dynamic between Yaakov and Esav, between the part of ourselves which seeks the good and the part of ourselves which is biased towards negativity. Rebbe Nachman, in Torah Aleph of sefer Likutey Moharan, couches the dynamic of Yaakov and Esav within the concept of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara. 

Ultimately, Yaakov’s mission is to take ownership of the birthright. Rebbe Nachman elucidates in Torah Aleph that the birthright corresponds to the concept of chochmah/wisdom. In our context, the part of ourselves which is rooted in Yaakov must claim the “birthright” that lives within us. That is to say, the aspect of our spiritual consciousness called “Yaakov” must take ownership of the inner wisdom which exists at the core of who we are. That point of inner wisdom is where the true self abides in all its possibility of what healthy living can look like. 

Perhaps, most profoundly, the “birthright” is constantly present within us. That inner point of wisdom which represents all the different facets of G dliness is never something outside of us. We just need the courage to take possession of that which has always been rightfully ours. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY

Parshat Chayei Sarah | Oct. 29-30, 2021

“Like a Phoenix”

By Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

(Dedicated to my two grandmothers who were niftar this past year, Sarah Esther bat Yaakov and Tzippora bat Yitzhak)

Rebbe Nachman’s main disciple, Rav Natan, wrote a phenomenal biography about his Rebbe titled, “Chayeh Moharan”, “The Life of our Master and Teacher, Nachman”. Rav Natan also wrote a raw and often vulnerable autobiography about himself titled “Yemot Moranat”, “The Days of our Master and Teacher, Natan”.

In explaining why Rav Natan used the term “Life” when dealing with his Rebbe, and “Days” when referring to himself, Rav Natan stated that all of his days joined together to produce one full life. But as for Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, every single day he had brand new life!

This constant, genuine renewal of life force for Rebbe Nachman was something wondrous and often inexplicable. However, Rebbe Nachman himself teaches the secret of his daily, Phoenix-like renewal.

In Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman states that the one common feature of all spiritual masters is that the only moment that exists for them is right now. They never ruminate about yesterday or contemplate tomorrow.

Instead, they throw themselves into the present moment with “all their heart, all their soul, and all their might”, as if it’s the only moment that has or will ever exist.

In this week’s Parsha, “Chayeh Sarah”, we learn about the unique life and passing of our foremother Sarah. Interestingly, the Torah states that she lived “100 years, and 20 years, and 7 years. These were the life of Sarah.”

All the Sages are busy trying to find the reason for the bizarre and seemingly unnecessary breakdown of the years of her life. Just say she lived until 127 years old and be done with it. “Yallah”, as my wife would say.

The Sages conclude that the Torah is highlighting that in every period of Sarah’s lifetime, she was truly alive. In this way, Sarah life was remarkable.

You might wrongly assume then that the life of Sarah must have been one of great grandeur and splendor. The truth is that Sarah’s life, like that of all the Tzaddikim, was often one of tremendous hardship and heartbreak.

Sarah was abducted and threatened to be molested on two separate occasions, not knowing if she would be saved from her scary predicament. Sarah’s one true aspiration was to have children, and yet this was the very thing she struggled with her whole life. As a result, Sarah had to standby and watch as her husband consorted with their maidservant, having a child together a full decade before Sarah had hers. The maidservant taunted Sarah regarding this predicament, leaving her frustrated and demoralized. Sarah’s life concluded when she faced the immanent death of her one son Yitzhak.

Yet with all of this, Sarah is the only person in the entire Torah to have a Parsha dedicated to the greatness of her life. Not Môshè Rabbeinu. Not David HaMelech. Not even Sarah’s husband Avraham Avinu. Only Sarah life was called “Life”.

The vital lesson we learn from this is that success in this world has nothing to do with being successful. The quality of ones life isn’t defined by the events that take place or the achievements one experiences. Instead, “The Tzaddik falls seven times and gets back up”. It is one’s resilience and refusal to stay down forever that serves as their true barometer for greatness. In this measure, Sarah was alive. In this measure. Rebbe Nachman was alive. And in this measure, we can all achieve true life as well.

May H” bless us with the courage and wisdom to understand that real success doesn’t preclude falling. Only that in the end, we get back up.

Like a Phoenix.

Like a Tzaddik.

Like Sarah.

Shabbat Shalom.

Selecting a Spouse

By Rabbi Benyamin Vineburg

Many of our readers, myself included, are or have recently been involved in shidduchim or dating relationships. The process of finding and selecting a soulmate is arduous, time consuming, vulnerable and, frankly, expensive. It takes a great deal of commitment and Emunah to do one’s due diligence, check references, travel for dates and be open and vulnerable a little more than usual.

This process, whether religious or secular, has become all the more difficult in a world where on-demand “feel goods” have replaced the need or desire for communication, understanding or hard work. In the United States, the divorce rates nears nearly 50%, not because we don’t have means to communicate or build relationships; social media has certainly taken care of that; but because we choose not to.

In this week’s parsha, Eliezer is sent by Avraham to find a wife for Yitzchak. Like any good Jewish parent, Avraham made sure to give Eliezer very specific requirements as to whom would be a suitable match. Eliezer is shown by Hashem a sign that Rivka, due to her kindness towards his animals and then him at the water well, is the right choice for Yitzchak.

I know what you’re thinking. I have asked Hashem for a sign for my own significant other too…where is my sign at the well? Perhaps Rivka’s actions can give us an answer.

Rivka embodied two incredible qualities; kindness and modesty. Many rabbaim and shadchanim remind us frequently of the importance of finding a baalat chesed and a tzinuah. She withdrew her external qualities in order to fully give of her internal qualities and it is those internal qualities that ultimately “got her the job.”

Many of us may be waiting for our sign at the well but we aren’t committed to looking at our perspective matches with the proper lens. I cannot count how many times I’ve had friends or students tell me that they refuse dates because of “their height”, “their body shape”, or “their upbringing.” Many dates are over before they’ve started because we have this twisted notion that our partner will resemble that of Johnny Depp or Angelina Jolie; and care very little for the substantive, realness of those we meet.

Rivka embodied qualities that we all can use to find our proper partners. She was kind and humble; giving first for giving sake and expecting nothing in return. She was modest, unpretentious and real; a quality that bodes well for a communicative and honest partner who will always seek to uplift rather than break down. She was calm and slow to anger; she had middot tovot, a solid foundation and grasp for who she was. These are the qualities to look for in a partner.

This week, exemplify the middot of Rivka. Give for giving’s sake. Be humble and modest. Look for the good in yourself and others. Have Emunah that Hashem will focus light upon you as you focus your light on others. Ask Hashem to give you a new or existing relationship with the qualities of Rivka, then, I pray, may you receive your sign and miracle speedily.

Good Shabbos.

By Aaron London, RN

My dear friends, I would like to share words of Torah with you this week that might be heavier than in past weeks.

In the days between the 12th and 16th of Tishrei, the Piaseczno Rebbe lost his son, his son’s wife, and his sister-in-law to the horrific Nazi air assults of September 1939. The Rebbe, who had begun to share divrei chizuk on Shabbos with his chasidim and anyone who was willing to listen, entered into a six-week silence (Abramson 78).

Then, on the Shabbos of November 4th, Parshas Chayei Sarah, the Rebbe spoke.

The Rebbe references a teaching found in sefer Ma’or va-Shemesh in the name of R’ Menacham Mendel of Rimanov. The Gemara in Brachos (5a) explains, “A covenant is made with salt, and a covenant is made with afflictions. Just as salt makes meat palatable, so too afflictions purify the individual of sins. The Ma’or va-Shemesh in the name of R’ Menacham Mendel of Rimanov comments, “Just as one cannot derive pleasure from meat that has been excessively salted, rather only if it was properly salted, so too afflictions should be meted out only in such measure that they can be tolerated, and with an admixture of mercy” (translation from R’ Henry Abramson’s Torah from the Years of Wrath, 80).

The Rebbe, utilizing the teaching of his great-grandfather, perceives a haunting chiddush in the Torah’s placement of Sarah’s death next to the Akeidas Yitzchak. Rashi comments, “the death of Sarah was juxtaposed to the binding of Yitzchak because with the news that her son was being bound and was about to be sacrificed, her soul burst forth from her and she died” (Bereshis 23:2). The Rebbe then explains that this juxtaposition was “in order to advocate for us, indicating what results from excessive afflictions, Heaven forbid – her soul burst forth” (80).

In his comments on this piece from the sefer Aish Kodesh, R’ Moshe Weinberger remarks that Sarah died form the horror of what might have been. She was broken from the unpredictability of life, of the uncertainty of each moment.

R’ Henry Abramson, in his work Torah from the Years of Wrath, which offers historical context in understanding the Torahs from sefer Aish Kodesh, comments, “It is difficult not to read an autobiographical perspective in this sermon – was the Rebbe not expressing a tiny part of his own ineffable anguish” (83)?

Indeed, as the Rebbe remarks, if Sarah Aminu who was a tzeddekas on the highest level, died out of the possibility of horror, what of us (the Rebbe ultimately explains that Sarah sacrificed herself for the Jewish people in order to convey to Hashem so-to-speak that the suffering was too much to bear)?

In the work I do with people who suffer from addiction, I often encounter those who have experienced some of the most unspeakable trauma. Sometimes, in a playful moment with my own daughter, my heart stops and I drift into a space where the residual energy of my patients surfaces to my mind and I shudder – what if… what if…. (lo aleinu).

There is the possibility of horror and horror itself and the trauma we all encounter in various degrees and intensities. How can we coexist with these two paradoxical notions – on the one hand the moment is uncertain and on the other hand, Hashem is lovingly guiding us through these very same moments to our ultimate tachlis? What happens when the moment is too much for us to bear?

My dear friends, it is here I tread on such delicate ground.

We engage with emunah at various ways. I can conceptually understand that everything Hashem does is for the good and for my ultimate benefit, but not feel that emunah within my emotional world. And, in the space inbetween my intellectual knowing and my emotional not-knowing, I encounter all the different expressions of inner turbulence.

R’ Joey Rosenfeld in the name of Rebbe Nachman and our tzaddikim will often mention the concept in his shiurim that the tachlis of knowing is not knowing, that the highest point of knowledge is for a person to ultimately admit that he does not and cannot truly know the essence of Hashem’s conduct. Perhaps, perched at the edge of a person’s conceptual recognition that everything emanates from Hashem, he then allows himself to fall into the vulnerability of not knowing. And, in his willingness to proclaim that he cannot understand the essence of why Hashem is doing this or that, he paradoxically allows his emotional world to fill with the simple emunah that Hashem is truly in control. A person, in his admittance, then says, “Hashem, I do not know. The moment is uncertain. And I am okay with not knowing.”

In truth, it is precisely through our ability to make a space for uncertainty that we offer ourselves the gift of okayness. I no longer have to resist the moment even though the moment is difficult or uncomfortable. Or, as I have heard R’ Rosenfeld mention, I can be okay even when things are not okay.

When we have the courage to be okay, we then open ourselves up to the possibility of redemption that lives within every moment.

Gut Shabbos,

A.L.Y

Parshat Lech Lecha | October 15-16, 2021

“Sarah’s Beauty”

Growing up, there were many obstacles I had to believing in the existence of G-d. Chief amongst them is why “bad things happen to good people”. This is a famous question and not one unique to me. It is a kasha that has been investigated for thousands of years by philosophers and theologians alike. In fact, Môshè Rabbeinu asked this very question to G-d Himself (Brachot 7a).

One of the problems with the question however, is the inherent and preconceived notion of what good is. When one begins to pour through Rebbe Nachman’s Torah, the assumed notion of good becomes flipped on its head and transformed. For the Rebbe, “good” is not what appears good or even what feels good. “Good” is nothing other than closeness to HaShem (Tehillim 73).

Once one internalizes real “good”, a paradigm shift begins to take place. What appeared to initially be “bad”; the events in our lives involving pain, cruelty, and trauma, chas v’shalom, ultimately becomes the very birth place of true good. For in truth, all distancing is only for the sake of being brought close (Likutey Moharan Tinyana 48)!

In Parshat Lech Lecha, this powerful dynamic comes to light. Our Sages teach us that Avraham’s life is a microcosm of every Jew’s life. And it is well documented that Avraham’s life was one of tremendous tests and challenges. I would like to examine one specific hardship which drives home the idea that apparent “bad” is merely concealed “good”.

HaShem had just communicated explicitly with Avraham for the first time, encouraging him to leave behind the comforts of his birthplace and trek to an unknown Land that only HaShem   could show him. However, as soon as Avraham arrives in Eretz Yisrael, a famine strikes and he is told to descend to Mitzrayim. This bizarre succession of events leads to the most unusual occurrence of all. 

As Avraham was taking his family down to Mitzrayim, the Torah points out that Avraham hadn’t truly appreciated how beautiful Sarah was. But they had been married for decades! The problematic nature of Avraham’s lack of perception is strengthened based on our Sages teaching that Sarah was one of the most beautiful women in history (Megillah 15A). Many answers are given by the commentators of the Torah to try and reconcile this difficulty, but none of them really leave you feeling satisfied.

Until a teaching of Rebbe Nachman dawned on me earlier this week. Rabbeinu teaches that Sarah uniquely embodies the quality of “Tefillah”, prayer, while Avraham embodies the “Tzaddik”, the lofty spiritual master (Likutey Moharan 10). Avraham and Sarah were inherently married, just as a Tzaddik is only a spiritual master due to his personal level of Tefillah. 

If we plug this secret in, we can begin to understand how Avraham, the Tzaddik, had never truly appreciated the tantalizing beauty of Sarah, Tefillah. The Gemara teaches that while prayer stands on the highest summit of existence, it is one of the things most overlooked by man (Brachot 6B). 

When does one begin to appreciate the incomparable beauty of prayer? 

Only when they go down to “Mitzrayim”, the place of suffering and servitude. 

I can vividly recall the most painful period of my life, sitting in a hospital bed after having checked myself into the local psych ward following three brutal years of major depression and debilitating psychosomatic symptoms. Through this period, it was only Rebbe Nachman’s Torah lessons and an indomitable willpower that had kept me alive. But to transition from barely surviving to truly living, I would need to come to the same realization as my forefather Avraham. That after all, Sarah really was beautiful. 

In my hospital gown with eyes stained from tears, I realized that the Torah, even the wisdom of Rebbe Nachman, could only allow me to survive. To live and thrive, I would need to actually take the Rebbe’s advice. I made a promise to HaShem from that day moving forward, I would actualize Rebbe Nachman’s greatest advice to us.

Sixty minutes of personal conversation a day with my Creator, speaking to HaShem as if He were my best friend. This was a practice I had previously held in contempt, but now it was my only hope left. I began to pour my heart to HaShem, throwing EVERYTHING on him, as if I had no where else to turn and no one else upon whom to rely (Sichot HaRan 2). 

Every sixty minutes of “Hitbodedut”, personal conversation with HaShem, took me out of another psycho-spiritual gate of despair. I began to recognize the transcendent beauty of Sarah. But it was only after having being sent down to my own personal “Mitzrayim”, that I could truly appreciate her. 

Avraham didn’t leave Mitzrayim empty-handed,  and neither had I. Avraham left laden with livestock. I left laden with real faith. All paradoxically accomplished through Sarah, heartfelt prayer. 

In a year in which we anxiously wait for our collective and personal Geulah, I bless each of us that we should work diligently and on a daily basis to cultivate Emunah through the daily practice of speaking to HaShem like He is your best friend. Because at the end of the day, Rabbeinu teaches that Redemption can only come about through Emunah, and Emunah can only be attained through Tefillah (Likutey Moharan 7). 

And lest you feel that this is a practice exclusive to Tzaddikim and therefore beyond your personal spiritual level, remember that the Torah refers to the Jewish people as “Kulam Tzaddikim”, all Tzaddikim. 

Every single Jew is a Tzaddik in potential. When you make an effort to recognize Sarah’s Beauty in your life, you will discover the Tzaddik inside of you and enter the Land that HaShem so desperately yearns to show you, the Land of Emunah!

Parshat Noach – October 8-9. 2021

Rise Above!

Rebbe Nachman teaches that the most important thing a Jew can do in their life is to find the spiritual master of the generation, and attach themselves to him. In fact, he says that your entire Judaism depends on it! (Likutey Moharan: 30)

Why is this task so crucial? And why does this teaching matter more now than ever?

Rebbe Nachman stated prophetically that a flood was about to pour into the world. However, as opposed to the floodwaters of Noach, this would be a torrential flood of atheism. And while the flood of Noach took lives, this flood would threaten to take something even more important, our faith. (Sichot HaRan: 35)

And while the Corona virus has swept over the world, affecting the lives of millions of people, Rebbe Nachman warns that the modern flood of atheism is actually the most damaging pandemic of all.

For the life force of a man, his joy, his hope, and even his health is intricately bound up and directly corresponding to the degree of faith he possesses. In fact, Rebbe Nachman teaches explicitly that there are illnesses that come upon a person only because of a “chesron b’emunah”, a lack of faith. (Likutey Moharan II: 5)

And this person can see the greatest of medical doctors and even the greatest tzaddikim of his time, and still not be cured of his illness. His healing, says Rebbe Nachman, will only come when he acquires genuine faith.

Therefore it should come as no surprise that in the modern age of atheism, rates of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, addiction, and use of psychiatric medications are sky rocketing. And no more so then in Western civilization where atheism is at its peak of power.

And this begs the ultimate question.

What’s the tikkun?

How does one brace themselves in the midst of the raging storm of atheism, and in the process protect those things that are most precious to him?

He must get on Noach’s ark. He must search tirelessly for the “Tzaddik Emet”, the True Tzaddik, and fight tooth and nail to attach himself to him. For only those most intimately connected to Noach survived the flood.

And herein lies that secret of Rebbe Nachman’s novel assertion that immediately prior to the coming of Mashiach, everyone would need him. (Chayah Moharan: 248 / 250)

Noach is referred to in the Zohar as the “Tzaddik Yesod Olam”, the spiritual master who serves as the literal foundation of the world. It is no coincidence that Rebbe Nachman, who is most commonly referred to in the same vein, the “Tzaddik Yesod Olam”, shares the same exact linguistic root as Noach!

Another tremendous allusion to the Tzaddik Emet being the only real refuge from the violent atheistic flood of our times, is that the only country which remained completely unscathed during the flood of Noach was the Land of Israel. Rebbe Nachman teaches that at their core, the Land ofIsrael and the Tzaddik Emet are identical. That by attaching oneself to the Tzaddik he has achieved the spiritual equivalent of physically living in the Land of Israel. (Likutey Moharan: 234)

In conclusion, Parshat Noach is not coming to tell us of the unlikely story of one family’s survival amidst a worldwide pandemic, but instead serves as a living, reverberating guide as to how one can presently rise above the modern floodwaters of atheism.

The final advice?

Find the Tzaddik.
